problems.title: Cat on a Plank
problems.summary: Find how far a cat can walk along an overhanging plank before the plank tips off the table.

a: As the cat walks out, the table’s support force on the plank shifts toward the edge. Where does it act at the moment the plank starts to tip?
Take torques about the table’s edge. The support force acts there, so it has no torque. Only the plank’s weight and the cat’s weight are left.
The centre of the plank is $$L/2-L/3=L/6$$ from the edge, on the table side. Balance $$Mg\,(L/6)$$ against $$mg\,x$$.
b: Use your result from part (a), $$x=ML/(6m)$$, with the numbers given.
The two masses appear as a ratio, so the kilograms cancel and $$x$$ comes out in metres.
Compare your answer with the length of the overhang, $$L/3=1.0\ \mathrm m$$. The tipping point has to be on the plank.
c: The cat cannot stand farther out than the end of the plank. How far past the edge is the end?
For the limiting cat, the tipping point of part (a) is exactly at the end, so $$x=L/3$$.
Set $$ML/(6m)=L/3$$ and solve for $$m$$. The length cancels.

problems.title: Two Sleds, One Rope
problems.summary: Two sleds on frictionless ice are pulled together by a rope. Find where they meet and how fast they close.

a: Look at both sleds as one system. Is there any horizontal force on it from outside? The rope pulls on both sleds, but it is part of the system.
No outside force and a start from rest mean the centre of mass stays where it is. So the sleds meet at the centre of mass.
Write $$m_Ad_A=m_Bd_B$$ and $$d_A+d_B=L$$, then solve for $$d_A$$.
b: The rope pulls each sled with the same force $$F$$. Each sled has a constant acceleration toward the other, $$F/m_A$$ and $$F/m_B$$.
The gap between the sleds closes with an acceleration equal to the sum of the two. It starts at $$L$$ with no closing speed.
Use $$u^2=2aL$$ with $$a=F/m_A+F/m_B$$. You can check with energy: Ayu’s hands do work $$FL$$ in total.

problems.title: Rough Ramp, Smooth Ramp
problems.summary: A ball rolls down a rough ramp and then climbs a frictionless one. Find its speed and how high it gets.

a: A ball that rolls has two kinds of kinetic energy, one from the motion of its centre and one from its spin.
Rolling without slipping links them through $$v=\omega r$$. Static friction does no work, so $$mgH$$ equals the total kinetic energy.
The spin energy is $$\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac25mr^2\omega^2=\tfrac15mv^2$$. So $$mgH=\tfrac7{10}mv^2$$.
b: Which forces act on the ball on the frictionless ramp? Ask whether either of them can change how fast the ball spins.
Gravity and the normal force both act along lines through the centre, so there is no torque. The spin stays the same all the way up.
Only $$\tfrac12mv^2$$ can turn into height. Set $$mgh=\tfrac12mv^2$$ with $$v$$ from part (a).
c: At the highest point the centre of the ball is at rest for a moment. Is the ball still spinning?
The spin energy at the top is the same as it was on the floor, $$\tfrac15mv^2$$.
Put in $$v^2=10gH/7$$ and divide by $$mgH$$. You can also subtract the answer to part (b) from 1.

problems.title: Hosing the Wall
problems.summary: Find the aim that lets a water jet reach the highest point on a wall, and how high that point is.

a: First find the height at which water aimed at angle $$\theta$$ hits the wall. The time to reach the wall is $$d/(v\cos\theta)$$.
You should get $$y=d\tan\theta-gd^2/(2v^2\cos^2\theta)$$. Use $$1/\cos^2\theta=1+\tan^2\theta$$ so that only $$\tan\theta$$ appears.
Now $$y$$ is a quadratic in $$\tan\theta$$ that opens downward. Its highest value is at the vertex.
b: Put the value of $$\tan\theta$$ from part (a) back into your expression for the height on the wall.
With $$T=v^2/(gd)$$, the term $$dT$$ becomes $$v^2/g$$ and the term with $$T^2$$ becomes $$v^2/(2g)$$.
Check your result at $$d=0$$. It should be the height of water shot straight up, $$v^2/(2g)$$.
c: Use your result from part (b) with the numbers given.
Work out the two terms one at a time: $$v^2/(2g)$$ and $$gd^2/(2v^2)$$.
Here $$v^2=196\ \mathrm{m^2/s^2}$$, so the first term is $$10\ \mathrm m$$. The second term is smaller than that.

problems.title: The Loading Voltmeter
problems.summary: A real voltmeter changes the voltage it measures. Find its reading and work back to its resistance.

a: A real voltmeter is a resistor. Connected across one resistor, it makes a parallel pair with it.
The pair has resistance $$R_p=RR_V/(R+R_V)$$. It is in series with the other resistor.
The battery voltage divides in proportion to resistance. The reading is $$V_0R_p/(R+R_p)$$. Simplify it.
b: Use your result from part (a). The reading divided by $$V_0$$ is $$4.0/9.0$$.
Write $$s=R_V/R$$. Your result from part (a) becomes $$s/(1+2s)$$.
Solve $$s/(1+2s)=4/9$$, which gives $$9s=4+8s$$. Then multiply by $$R$$.
c: Draw the new circuit. Each resistor now has the same kind of voltmeter across it.
The two halves of the circuit are identical and in series. How does the battery voltage divide between them?
Each half gets half of $$9.0\ \mathrm V$$. You do not need $$R_V$$ for this part.

problems.title: The Magnetic Slab
problems.summary: A charged particle enters a slab of uniform magnetic field. Find when it gets through, how far it turns and how long it takes.

a: The magnetic force is always at right angles to the velocity. What kind of path does that give, and what happens to the speed?
The path is a circle of radius $$r=mv/(qB)$$. The particle enters at right angles to the face, so the centre of the circle lies in that face.
The circle reaches a depth $$r$$ into the slab at most. The particle gets through when $$r$$ is larger than $$d$$.
b: Twice the speed means twice the radius. So $$r=2d$$.
When the velocity has turned through an angle $$\theta$$, the particle is at a depth $$r\sin\theta$$ inside the slab. A sketch of the circle and its centre helps.
The particle leaves at depth $$d$$, so $$\sin\theta=d/r=1/2$$.
c: The speed is constant on the arc. You can use arc length divided by speed, or the turning angle divided by the angular rate.
The angular rate is $$\omega=v/r=qB/m$$. It does not depend on the speed.
Use $$t=\theta/\omega$$ with the angle of part (b) in radians, $$\theta=\pi/6$$.

problems.title: Two Charges Head On
problems.summary: One charged bead is fired at another that is free to move. Find their closest approach and the final speeds.

a: Think about the gap between the beads. It shrinks while bead A is faster than bead B and grows once bead B is faster.
So at the closest approach both beads have the same velocity. Bead B is not at rest then.
Momentum is conserved because the only forces are between the beads. Write $$mv=(m+3m)u$$.
b: Energy is conserved. Compare the start, where the beads are very far apart, with the moment of closest approach.
At closest approach both beads move at $$v/4$$, so the kinetic energy then is $$\tfrac12(4m)(v/4)^2=\tfrac18mv^2$$.
The rest of the starting kinetic energy is stored as $$kq^2/r$$. So $$kq^2/r=\tfrac12mv^2-\tfrac18mv^2$$.
c: Long after, the beads are far apart and the potential energy is zero again. Which two quantities are back at their starting values?
Momentum and kinetic energy are both conserved from start to end. That is a head-on elastic collision between masses $$m$$ and $$3m$$.
Use $$mv=mv_A+3mv_B$$ together with $$v_B-v_A=v$$, the rule that the beads separate as fast as they approached.

problems.title: Round the Funnel
problems.summary: Two balls circle inside a smooth funnel at different heights. Find the speed, compare the periods and find when the balls line up again.

a: Two forces act on the ball, its weight and the normal force from the wall. Which way does the normal force point?

The normal force makes an angle $$\alpha$$ with the horizontal. Its vertical part balances the weight and its horizontal part keeps the ball on the circle: $$N\sin\alpha=mg$$ and $$N\cos\alpha=mv^2/r$$.
Divide one equation by the other and use $$r=h\tan\alpha$$ for the radius of the circle. The angle cancels.
b: The period is the distance round the circle divided by the speed, $$T=2\pi r/v$$.
Both $$r$$ and $$v$$ depend on the height. Use $$r=h\tan\alpha$$ and $$v=\sqrt{gh}$$ to see how $$T$$ depends on $$h$$.
The period is proportional to $$\sqrt h$$. The upper ball is four times as high.
c: The two balls go round at different rates. Which one goes round faster?
The lower ball has angular rate $$\omega=2\pi/T$$ and the upper ball has half of that. They line up again when the lower ball has gained one full turn.
The lower ball gains at the rate $$\omega/2$$, so the time is $$2\pi/(\omega/2)=2T$$, with $$T=2\pi\tan\alpha\sqrt{h/g}$$.

problems.title: The Rectangular Cycle
problems.summary: A monatomic ideal gas goes round a rectangle on the pressure and volume diagram. Find the work, the heat taken in and the efficiency.

a: The gas does work only on the legs where its volume changes. Which two legs are those?
At constant pressure the work done by the gas is $$p\,\Delta V$$. It is positive on the expansion and negative on the compression.
Add $$2p_0(3V_0-V_0)$$ and $$-p_0(3V_0-V_0)$$. The result is the area of the rectangle.
b: Treat each leg on its own with the first law, $$Q=\Delta U+W$$, and $$U=\tfrac32pV$$.
Decide the sign of $$Q$$ on each leg. Heat flows in where the product $$pV$$ rises, which here is on AB and BC.
You should find $$Q_{AB}=\tfrac32p_0V_0$$ and $$Q_{BC}=6p_0V_0+4p_0V_0$$. Add these two only.
c: The efficiency is the net work of part (a) divided by the heat taken in of part (b).
Do not divide by the net heat of the whole cycle. That always equals the work.
The factors $$p_0V_0$$ cancel, leaving $$2$$ divided by $$23/2$$.

problems.title: A Lamp Under a Raft
problems.summary: A raft floats above an underwater lamp. Find how large the raft must be to stop all the lamp’s light leaving the water.

a: Follow rays from the lamp that hit the surface farther and farther from the point above the lamp. How does their angle to the normal change?
Past the critical angle the light is totally reflected. So light leaves the water only inside a circle of radius $$h\tan\theta_c$$, and the raft has to cover it.
The critical angle has $$\sin\theta_c=1/n$$. Turn that into $$\tan\theta_c=1/\sqrt{n^2-1}$$.
b: Use your result from part (a) with the numbers given.
The square root of $$7/9$$ is about $$0.882$$. Divide the depth by it.
c: The same relation links the radius and the depth. Now the radius is known and the depth is not.
A deeper lamp lights a wider circle on the surface. So the raft works for every depth up to a limit.
Solve the result of part (a) for the depth, $$h=R\sqrt{n^2-1}$$.

problems.title: Walking Past Two Speakers
problems.summary: Two speakers play the same tone. Count the quiet points on a walk away from one of them and find the last one.

a: The listener, $$S_1$$ and $$S_2$$ make a right-angled triangle. How far is the listener from $$S_2$$?
The path difference is $$\Delta=\sqrt{x^2+d^2}-x$$. To solve for $$x$$, move $$x$$ to the other side before you square.
Squaring $$\Delta+x=\sqrt{x^2+d^2}$$ gives $$\Delta^2+2\Delta x=d^2$$. The $$x^2$$ terms cancel.
b: Find the wavelength first. Then ask which path differences make the two sounds cancel.
The sounds cancel when $$\Delta$$ is half a wavelength, one and a half wavelengths, and so on. Which values does $$\Delta$$ take along the walk?
The path difference starts at $$d=3.0\ \mathrm m$$ and falls toward zero without reaching it. Count the cancelling values in that range.
c: The path difference keeps falling along the walk. So the last quiet point has the smallest cancelling path difference.
That value is half a wavelength, $$\Delta=0.5\ \mathrm m$$.
Put $$d=3.0\ \mathrm m$$ and $$\Delta=0.5\ \mathrm m$$ into your result from part (a).

problems.title: Two Isotopes, One Sample
problems.summary: A sample holds two isotopes with different half-lives. Compare their numbers of nuclei and their activities as time passes.

a: After each half-life, half of the nuclei that were there are left.
Count the half-lives in $$6.0\ \mathrm h$$. Isotope X has had three and isotope Y has had one.
The fractions left are $$1/8$$ and $$1/2$$. The starting numbers are equal, so divide one fraction by the other.
b: Activity is decays per second. It depends on how many nuclei there are and on how likely each one is to decay.
Use $$A=\lambda N$$ with $$\lambda=\ln2/T$$, where $$T$$ is the half-life. The shorter half-life has the larger decay constant.
The ratio is $$(T_Y/T_X)(N_X/N_Y)$$. The first factor is 3 and the second is your answer to part (a).
c: Write the activity ratio at a general time $$t$$ in hours, using $$N=N_02^{-t/T}$$ for each isotope.
The ratio is $$3\times2^{-t/2}/2^{-t/6}=3\times2^{-t/3}$$. It starts at 3 and falls.
Set the ratio equal to 1, so $$2^{t/3}=3$$. Take logarithms to get $$t=3\ln3/\ln2$$.

problems.title: Ice in the Flask
problems.summary: Cold ice goes into a flask of warm water. Work out the final state, with the flask’s own heat capacity included.

a: You do not know the final state yet. It could be all water, ice and water together at $$0\ ^\circ\mathrm C$$, or all ice. Test them against the heat available.

The water and the flask cool together and give up $$1330\ \mathrm J$$ for each kelvin. Cooling to $$0\ ^\circ\mathrm C$$ gives $$39\,900\ \mathrm J$$. The ice needs $$6300\ \mathrm J$$ to warm to $$0\ ^\circ\mathrm C$$ before any of it melts.
The heat left for melting is $$39\,900-6300=33\,600\ \mathrm J$$. Divide by the latent heat to get the mass that melts, then subtract from $$150\ \mathrm g$$.
b: In the limiting case all the ice has just melted and everything ends as water at $$0\ ^\circ\mathrm C$$.
The ice needs $$6300\ \mathrm J$$ to warm up and $$50\,400\ \mathrm J$$ to melt, $$56\,700\ \mathrm J$$ in all.
The water and the flask give up $$1330\ \mathrm J$$ for each kelvin they cool. Set $$1330\,T=56\,700$$.
c: The heat available is the same as in part (a), $$39\,900\ \mathrm J$$. Now the mass of ice is the unknown.
Each kilogram of ice needs $$42\,000\ \mathrm J$$ to warm to $$0\ ^\circ\mathrm C$$ and $$336\,000\ \mathrm J$$ to melt.
Divide $$39\,900\ \mathrm J$$ by $$378\,000\ \mathrm{J/kg}$$ and convert to grams.

problems.title: The Unknown Pipe
problems.summary: Two resonances of a pipe are known, with one more between them. Work out what kind of pipe it is, its fundamental and its length.

a: There are two kinds of pipe to test. One open at both ends resonates at every whole-number multiple of its fundamental. One closed at one end resonates at the odd multiples only.
With exactly one resonance between them, the two given frequencies are two steps apart. A step is $$f_1$$ for an open pipe and $$2f_1$$ for a pipe closed at one end.
The open pipe would give $$f_1=170\ \mathrm{Hz}$$, but $$255/170$$ is not a whole number. Try the pipe closed at one end and check that both frequencies are odd multiples.
b: Part (a) also told you what kind of pipe this is. How much of a wavelength fits in that kind of pipe in its fundamental?
For a pipe closed at one end, a quarter of a wavelength fits, so $$L=\lambda/4$$.
Use $$\lambda=v/f_1$$ with $$f_1=85\ \mathrm{Hz}$$, then divide by 4.
c: With the cap off the pipe is open at both ends. Its length has not changed.
In the fundamental of a pipe open at both ends, half a wavelength fits in the pipe.
Use $$f=v/(2L)$$ with the length from part (b).

problems.title: Two Colours, One Cathode
problems.summary: One cathode is lit by two kinds of light. Use one stopping voltage and a wavelength ratio to find the work function and the wavelength.

a: Write the photoelectric equation once for each light: photon energy equals work function plus the kinetic energy of the fastest electrons. The stopping voltage gives that kinetic energy as $$eV_1$$.
Twice the speed means four times the kinetic energy. The second photon has $$\tfrac53$$ of the energy of the first, because its wavelength is $$\tfrac35$$ as long.
You now have $$hc/\lambda=\phi+eV_1$$ and $$\tfrac53\,hc/\lambda=\phi+4eV_1$$. Put the first into the second and solve for $$\phi$$.
b: Use your result from part (a) with $$V_1=0.60\ \mathrm V$$.
An electron that crosses $$0.60\ \mathrm V$$ gains or loses $$0.60\ \mathrm{eV}$$, so $$eV_1=0.60\ \mathrm{eV}$$.
Multiply $$0.60\ \mathrm{eV}$$ by $$7/2$$.
c: Find the photon energy of the first light from its photoelectric equation.
The photon energy is the work function plus $$eV_1$$, which is $$2.10\ \mathrm{eV}+0.60\ \mathrm{eV}$$.
Divide $$hc=1240\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}$$ by the photon energy in electronvolts.
